function.one_sentence_plain_english: This is the brain of the kit: a small board that runs the program you write and controls every wire connected to it.
function.what_it_is_used_for: It reads sensors, decides what to do based on your code, and sends signals out to turn on lights, spin motors, move servos, and more.
function.how_it_works_briefly: A chip called the ATmega328P stores and runs your program. It talks to your computer over USB through a second small chip (a USB-to-serial converter) so you can load new code and see debug messages.

pins.pin_1_identification: There is no single numbered pin 1. Orientation is found by locating the USB-B connector and the round DC barrel jack, which sit together on one short edge of the board; the power header (VIN/GND/5V/3V3/IOREF/RESET) is printed on the same edge.

electrical.operating_voltage: 5V logic (on-board 5V regulator output)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: 20V on the VIN barrel jack (Arduino Uno Rev3 input voltage limit); exceeding this risks damaging the onboard regulator
electrical.typical_current: roughly 45-50 mA idle board draw; varies with attached peripherals (rule-of-thumb figure, not independently confirmed for the ELEGOO clone)
electrical.max_current: 20 mA max per digital I/O pin, 50 mA max on the 3.3V pin (official Arduino Uno Rev3 spec, assumed to apply to the ELEGOO clone)
electrical.logic_level: 5V TTL/CMOS
electrical.interface: digital, analog (ADC), PWM, UART, I2C, SPI (multi-interface microcontroller board)

key_specs.usb_to_serial_chip: CH340C (standalone ELEGOO board, confirmed) or ATMEGA16U2 (some kit bundle revisions, per Amazon listing)
key_specs.board_dimensions_mm: 68.6 x 53.4 (official Arduino Uno Rev3 reference dimensions)

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Rectangular PCB about 7 cm x 5.5 cm, with a USB-B port and a round DC barrel power jack on one short edge, and a row of black plastic pin-header sockets along each long edge.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Most ELEGOO boards are blue soldermask (some are black); a black rectangular IC sits in the middle (either a wide DIP-28 through-hole chip or a small square surface-mount chip, depending on revision); a small silver 3-legged crystal/resonator sits near it; a small square reset button is near the USB port; a few tiny surface-mount LEDs sit near the USB connector (a steady power LED and a blinking TX/RX pair).
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Silkscreen reads "UNO R3", "ARDUINO" or "ELEGOO" plus pin labels above each header: POWER (IOREF, RESET, 3V3, 5V, GND, GND, VIN), ANALOG IN (A0-A5), and DIGITAL (AREF, GND, D13 down to D0, with a tilde ~ before PWM-capable pin numbers).
easily_confused_with: Arduino Mega 2560 (larger board, many more pins)
other-brand Uno R3 clones with an identical header layout
ELEGOO Mega board

required_extra_parts: USB cable (to program or power from a computer)
9V battery or 7-12V power adapter (for stand-alone operation)
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none required; use the standard Arduino IDE and its built-in functions (pinMode, digitalWrite, analogRead, etc.)

hazards: Reversed-polarity power into the barrel jack (center must be positive) can damage the board
Static discharge can damage exposed chip pins
Shorting 5V to GND on the header can overheat the onboard regulator
handling_notes: Hold the board by the edges of the PCB
Do not touch chip legs or header pins with wet hands
Unplug USB power before attaching or removing a shield
common_mistakes: Feeding more than the rated ~20V into the barrel jack
Drawing more than 20 mA from a single digital pin (for example wiring an LED with no series resistor)
Uploading code while something else is driving D0/D1 (RX/TX), which interferes with the USB programming connection

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Board not recognized by the computer
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Missing USB driver for the CH340 or ATMEGA16U2 chip, or a bad USB cable
symptoms_and_causes.check: Check Device Manager (Windows) or System Information (macOS) for a COM/serial port when plugged in

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Power LED not lit
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: No power reaching the board (bad cable, reversed barrel-jack polarity, blown regulator)
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure voltage between the 5V and GND header pins with a multimeter

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Code uploads but nothing happens
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Wrong board or COM port selected in the IDE, or a bug in the sketch
symptoms_and_causes.check: Re-select "Arduino Uno" and the correct port in the IDE, then re-upload

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the board powered (USB or barrel jack), set the meter to DC volts and measure between the 5V pin and any GND pin; expect close to 5.0V. Measure between 3V3 and GND for close to 3.3V.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small screen that displays two lines of up to 16 letters or numbers, so your project can show text instead of just blinking lights.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Showing sensor readings, menus, a clock, or status messages from your Arduino program.

pins.pin_1_identification: Pin 1 (VSS/ground) is the end of the 16-hole header nearest the display's mounting corner; confirm against the printed pin numbers or a dot marker next to the header, since header orientation can vary slightly by board revision.

electrical.operating_voltage: 4.7V to 5.3V (module VDD, per common 1602 module datasheets); the underlying HD44780 controller IC itself is rated 2.7V-5.5V (VCC) per the Hitachi/Renesas datasheet
electrical.typical_current: about 1 mA for the logic/controller alone, not including the backlight
electrical.max_current: backlight LED typically draws roughly 80-120 mA at 5V through a series resistor (reference figure only; not confirmed from a fetched datasheet for this exact module)
electrical.logic_level: 5V TTL

key_specs.backlight_color: blue (white-on-blue is the common variant; yellow-green also common)
key_specs.contrast_control: external potentiometer required, wired to the V0 pin

visual_identification.shape_and_size: A rectangular glass display window (roughly 80mm x 36mm) mounted on a slightly larger PCB, with a single row of 16 pin holes along the bottom edge. The kit's "with pin header" label means a straight breakaway male header ships either pre-soldered or loose alongside it.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Screen background is usually solid blue or blue-green with white or black characters when lit; the PCB is typically green or blue.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Silkscreen near the header often reads "1602A" or similar, with pin numbers 1-16 printed above or below the header holes.
easily_confused_with: 16x2 LCD with an I2C backpack (only 4 pins: GND, VCC, SDA, SCL, plus a small blue potentiometer on a separate small board)
20x4 LCD modules (larger, 4 lines)
monochrome graphic LCDs (128x64, no visible character grid lines)

required_extra_parts: 10K potentiometer (for contrast)
current-limiting resistor for the backlight if not already on the module (commonly around 220 ohm)
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: LiquidCrystal (built into the Arduino IDE)

hazards: Backlight can get warm with prolonged use
Reversing VDD/VSS can damage the controller chip
Forcing current through the backlight the wrong way can damage the LED
handling_notes: Handle by the PCB edges, avoid pressing on the glass display area
Keep RW tied to GND unless your code actually reads the busy flag
common_mistakes: Forgetting the contrast potentiometer, which makes the screen look blank or full of black boxes
Wiring RS and E backwards
Leaving RW floating instead of grounded, which can cause erratic behavior

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Screen is blank but backlight is on
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Contrast (V0) not adjusted, or wrong pin numbers in code
symptoms_and_causes.check: Turn the contrast potentiometer while the board is powered; you should see rows of black boxes appear

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Backlight does not light at all
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: No power reaching VDD/VSS or the backlight pins, or reversed backlight polarity
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure voltage between VDD and VSS with a multimeter; expect about 5V

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Garbled or random characters
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Wrong wiring on the data pins (D4-D7) or RS/E, or the sketch is set up for the wrong pin mapping
symptoms_and_causes.check: Double check each data pin against the sketch's LiquidCrystal() constructor pin list

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the module powered, measure DC voltage between VDD (pin 2) and VSS (pin 1); expect about 5V. Measure between A (pin 15) and K (pin 16) for the backlight supply; expect close to the supply voltage minus the resistor's voltage drop.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A blank circuit board that plugs on top of the UNO and gives you a small breadboard and solder pads, so you can build a circuit without a tangle of loose wires.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Building semi-permanent or compact circuits: stick components onto the small breadboard on top for a solderless build, or solder parts directly onto the prototyping grid underneath for something sturdier.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The shield's header pins on the underside plug straight into the Uno's own headers, extending every Uno pin up to a matching row of holes on top of the shield right next to the mini breadboard, so wiring a part is a short hop instead of a long wire run.

pins.pin_1_identification: There is no dedicated pin 1. Orientation is fixed because the header spacing only stacks onto an Uno one way, keyed against the USB/power-jack end of the Uno like any other shield.

electrical.operating_voltage: same as whatever the Uno underneath supplies (5V logic at the shield's header)
electrical.typical_current: negligible; the shield's own onboard LED circuit draws a few mA when used
electrical.logic_level: 5V TTL (inherited from the Uno)
electrical.interface: none (passive pass-through board, no chip of its own)

key_specs.onboard_extras: 2 LEDs (red, green) each with a matching resistor, 1 reset button, 1 general-purpose push button, two 0.1uF capacitors, a surface-mount pad area for chips up to 14-pin SOIC, gold-plated header pads, 0.1in x 0.1in prototyping grid, and a pass-through ICSP header so another shield can stack on top

visual_identification.shape_and_size: A rectangular PCB the same footprint as the Uno (about 7cm x 5.5cm) with two rows of female header sockets on the underside that plug straight down onto the Uno's pins, and a small breadboard (about 4.8cm x 3.4cm) stuck on top with its own grid of tiny insertion holes.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: PCB color usually matches other boards in the kit (commonly blue or red); the mini breadboard on top is white plastic with a printed red stripe (positive rail) and blue stripe (negative rail) along its edges.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: A grid of prototyping pads near the header edges, plus a small reset button and an unlabeled general-purpose push button near one corner.
easily_confused_with: A full-size solderless breadboard (much bigger, no header pins to plug into a board)
A bare Uno shield with no breadboard on top
A perfboard/stripboard (bare copper pads, no adhesive breadboard on top)

required_extra_parts: jumper wires or direct component leads to use the mini breadboard or solder pads
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none; it is a passive board

hazards: Misaligning the header pins when pressing the shield onto the Uno can bend a pin
Careless soldering on the prototyping grid can bridge adjacent pads and short a signal to power or ground
handling_notes: Line up the header sockets carefully before pressing down; press evenly, not on one corner
Unplug USB power before attaching or removing the shield
common_mistakes: Assuming the mini breadboard's power rails are automatically connected to the Uno's 5V/GND (they are not, until you jumper them yourself)
Forgetting the shield adds height, which can make some enclosures not fit

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Nothing on the shield's breadboard works
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: The breadboard's power rails were never jumpered to the Uno's 5V/GND pins
symptoms_and_causes.check: Run a jumper wire from a 5V pin on the shield header to the breadboard's + rail, and GND to the - rail, then re-check

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Uno stops responding after attaching the shield
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: A bent or misaligned header pin is shorting two signals together
symptoms_and_causes.check: Remove the shield and inspect the header pins for bending before reseating

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the shield seated and the Uno powered, measure continuity between any GND point on the shield's header and the Uno's own GND pin; you should read near 0 ohm, confirming a solid connection.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A little board that turns a 9V battery or wall adapter into clean, steady 5V and 3.3V power for your breadboard circuits.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Powering breadboard circuits without needing the Uno or a USB cable connected; useful when you want a project to run on its own.
function.how_it_works_briefly: It takes power in through a barrel jack or USB port, then uses onboard voltage regulators to produce steady 3.3V and 5V outputs, feeding them out to the breadboard's power rails through two pairs of pins that you select with small jumpers.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small circuit board that acts like a strong relay for weak signals, letting the tiny electrical pulses from an Arduino control a motor that needs far more current than the Arduino can supply directly.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Driving the 28BYJ-48 stepper motor (or other small 4-phase unipolar stepper motors, or other inductive loads like relays and lamps) from a microcontroller.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside is a ULN2003 chip containing seven Darlington transistor pairs. Each pair works like a switch: a small current from an Arduino IN pin flips the switch, letting a much bigger current from the external power supply flow through one motor coil at a time in the right sequence.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small motor that turns in fixed, precise steps instead of spinning freely, so a microcontroller can command an exact rotation and know where the shaft ended up without any extra position sensor.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Precise positioning tasks such as camera pan/tilt rigs, clock hands, valve actuators, and small mechanisms that need to move a known amount and hold position.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Four internal coils are energized in sequence, and each energizing step pulls a geared magnetic rotor forward by a small fixed angle. A built-in gearbox (about 64:1) turns many small internal steps into one much finer, stronger step at the output shaft.

wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: Stepper.h (built into the Arduino IDE) or AccelStepper (third-party)

hazards: very low voltage, no shock hazard
the internal gearbox can be damaged by forcing the shaft to turn by hand while powered, or by stalling it against a hard stop for a long time
handling_notes: don't force or over-tighten anything onto the thin 5mm output shaft
the 5-pin connector is keyed and only seats correctly one way into the driver board's socket
common_mistakes: trying to power the motor directly from an Arduino pin instead of through the driver board (it draws far more current than a pin can safely supply)
mixing up full-step and half-step code and expecting 4096 steps per revolution while running full-step mode (which only gives 2048)

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: motor buzzes or vibrates without turning
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: one of the 4 coil wires is loose or swapped, or the code's step sequence doesn't match the wiring
symptoms_and_causes.check: reseat the connector fully and verify the library's step table matches the coil wire order

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: motor turns the opposite direction from what's expected
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: the coil order is effectively reversed relative to what the code assumes
symptoms_and_causes.check: flip the sign of the step count in code rather than rewiring the connector

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: motor stalls or skips steps under light load
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: the driver board is being powered from the Arduino's onboard 5V regulator, which can't supply enough current under load
symptoms_and_causes.check: power the driver board's '+' pin from a separate 5V supply and confirm current draw with a multimeter in series

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the motor disconnected from the driver board, measure resistance between the Red wire and each of Orange/Pink/Yellow/Blue in turn; each should read roughly 50 ohm (per the coil resistance spec) and be close to equal across all four. An infinite (open) reading on any pair indicates a broken coil wire.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small motor that moves to whatever angle you tell it and holds that position, instead of spinning continuously like a normal motor.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Robot arms, steering for small RC cars, pan/tilt camera mounts, and any project that needs something to swing to a precise position and stay there.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the plastic case is a small DC motor, a set of reduction gears, and a tiny circuit board with a position sensor (a potentiometer). The circuit compares the angle you asked for, which is encoded as a repeating electrical pulse, against the actual position, and drives the motor until the two match.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: An electrically controlled switch: a small 5V signal flips an internal lever that opens or closes a completely separate, much bigger circuit.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Turning higher-voltage or higher-current things, like a lamp, a fan, or a wall-powered appliance, on and off using a low-power signal from an Arduino, without ever wiring the Arduino directly into that higher-power circuit.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Sending current through the relay's internal coil creates a small magnetic field that pulls a metal lever (the armature) from one contact to another, similar to a person flipping a switch by hand, except triggered electrically, with the coil side and the switched side kept electrically isolated from each other.

pinout.name: Coil pin A
pinout.notes: one coil terminal; the coil has no fixed positive/negative side

pinout.notes: other coil terminal

pinout.notes: the moving contact; connects to whichever of NO or NC is currently closed

pinout.name: NO
pinout.notes: connected to COM only while the coil is energized

pinout.name: NC
pinout.notes: connected to COM only while the coil is NOT energized

pins.pin_1_identification: The two coil pins sit on one side of the case and the three switch pins (COM, NO, NC) sit on the opposite side; the datasheet's wiring diagram shows this layout but the case markings can wear off, so confirming with a multimeter continuity check is recommended before wiring.

electrical.operating_voltage: 5V DC (coil)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: 120% of nominal, i.e. about 6V max allowable coil voltage, per the Songle SRD datasheet; the switched side is separately rated up to 250VAC/30VDC depending on load type
electrical.typical_current: 71.4 mA nominal coil current, per the Songle SRD datasheet
electrical.max_current: 10A switched load (resistive, 125VAC or 28VDC, Form C rating) or 7A at 240VAC, per the Songle SRD datasheet; the coil itself is not meant to carry more than its rated ~71 mA
electrical.logic_level: the coil needs its full 71 mA at 5V, which is more than a single Arduino pin should supply directly, so a transistor stage is normally used to switch it rather than driving it from a pin directly
electrical.interface: digital, switched through a transistor driver stage rather than a microcontroller pin directly

key_specs.coil_resistance: 70 ohm, per the Songle SRD datasheet
key_specs.coil_power: 0.36 W, per the Songle SRD datasheet
key_specs.contact_form: SPDT / Form C (one common contact, one normally-open, one normally-closed)
key_specs.contact_resistance: 100 milliohm max, per the Songle SRD datasheet
key_specs.dielectric_strength_coil_to_contact: 1500 VAC for 1 minute, per the Songle SRD datasheet
key_specs.operate_release_time: operate time 10 ms max, release time 5 ms max, per the Songle SRD datasheet
key_specs.mechanical_life: 10,000,000 operations minimum with no load, per the Songle SRD datasheet
key_specs.electrical_life: 100,000 operations minimum at rated load, per the Songle SRD datasheet

visual_identification.shape_and_size: small blue rectangular plastic block roughly 19 mm x 16 mm x 16 mm, sitting on 5 metal pins that poke out the bottom
visual_identification.color_and_markings: blue plastic housing, usually printed with 'SONGLE' and 'SRD-05VDC-SL-C', plus small print showing ratings like '10A 250VAC'; some versions have a small clear window on top showing the internal contacts
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: 'SRD-05VDC-SL-C' or a similar part code printed on top; '5VDC' near one corner; UL/CUL/TUV certification marks near the ratings text
easily_confused_with: other Songle relay voltage variants that look identical except for the printed voltage code (e.g. SRD-12VDC-SL-C, SRD-24VDC-SL-C)
at a glance, a large blue capacitor, though the relay is bigger and has 5 pins rather than 2 leads

example_connections.uno_pin: 5V supply (through the load side of a transistor switch, not wired straight to a digital pin)
transistor collector (e.g. PN2222), with the transistor's emitter to GND and its base driven from a digital pin through a resistor
one side of the external switched circuit; not connected to the Arduino
other side of the external switched circuit, chosen based on whether the load should default to off (use NO) or on (use NC) when unpowered

required_extra_parts: an NPN transistor (e.g. PN2222) to switch the coil current, since an Arduino pin alone cannot safely supply the coil's ~71 mA
a flyback diode (e.g. 1N4007) across the coil to protect the transistor from the voltage spike created when the coil turns off
a base resistor (commonly around 1 kOhm) between the Arduino pin and the transistor base
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none required; controlled with digitalWrite()

hazards: if the switched (COM/NO/NC) side is wired to mains voltage, that side becomes genuinely dangerous and can shock or kill; treat any such wiring as a live circuit
without a flyback diode across the coil, switching it off can generate a voltage spike that damages the driving transistor or a microcontroller pin
handling_notes: never touch the COM/NO/NC pins or their wiring while the load side is connected to mains power
confirm which pins are coil versus switch contacts with a multimeter before wiring; they are electrically isolated but physically close together on the case
common_mistakes: trying to drive the coil directly from an Arduino digital pin without a transistor stage
omitting the flyback diode across the coil
wiring the load to NC when NO was intended, leaving the load powered on by default instead of off

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: relay never clicks
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: the transistor isn't switching, or the coil wiring is broken
symptoms_and_causes.check: measure DC voltage across the coil pins when the control signal is HIGH; it should read close to 5V

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: relay clicks but the switched circuit doesn't turn on
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: the load is wired to NC instead of NO, or there's a broken wire in the switched circuit
symptoms_and_causes.check: with the coil unpowered, use continuity mode between COM and NC (should beep); with the coil powered, use continuity mode between COM and NO (should beep only then)

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: the driving transistor or an Arduino pin gets warm or fails after repeated switching
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: a missing flyback diode across the coil
symptoms_and_causes.check: add a 1N4007 diode across the coil pins, with its cathode band toward the positive supply side

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With no power connected, set the multimeter to resistance/continuity mode. Between the two coil pins you should read roughly 70 ohm. Between COM and NC you should read continuity (near 0 ohm) while unpowered; between COM and NO you should read continuity only once 5V is applied across the coil pins.

function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the black dome is a photodiode tuned to see only light that blinks 38,000 times per second (38 kHz), the flicker rate used by most IR remotes. A small chip inside filters out sunlight and lamp flicker, then outputs a clean digital pulse train that matches the remote's code.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A thumbstick you can push in any direction, plus a hidden button when you press straight down, that tells the Arduino which way it's tilted.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Steering a robot, moving a cursor, or controlling motor speed and direction by hand.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Two small potentiometers (variable resistors), one for left-right and one for forward-back, are linked to the stick. Each forms a voltage divider: when the stick is centered, its output sits at about half the supply voltage; tilting it raises or lowers that voltage. Pressing the stick straight down closes a separate momentary switch that connects its pin to ground.

pinout.name: Button (SW)
pinout.notes: Connects to GND when the stick is pressed down; needs a pull-up (use Arduino's INPUT_PULLUP)

pinout.name: Y-position (VRy)
pinout.notes: Voltage from 0 to VCC depending on forward/back tilt

pinout.name: X-position (VRx)
pinout.notes: Voltage from 0 to VCC depending on left/right tilt

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small sensor that tells the Arduino how warm it is and how humid the air is.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Reading room temperature and relative humidity, for example for a weather display, an incubator, or a greenhouse controller.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the blue plastic block is a humidity-sensing film and a small temperature sensor, plus a tiny chip that measures both and sends the readings out as a timed digital pulse pattern on a single data wire, about once per second.

pinout.name: DATA
pinout.notes: Serial data for both temperature and humidity; the module has a built-in pull-up resistor

key_specs.temperature_accuracy: +/-1C per the fetched module datasheet (some Aosong bare-chip datasheets state +/-2C; treat +/-1-2C as the realistic accuracy band)
key_specs.sampling_period: 1 reading per second minimum; many libraries recommend waiting 2 seconds between reads for reliable data

hazards: None; low voltage, low current sensor
handling_notes: Avoid getting the sensor wet or breathing on it at close range for long periods, since this can affect long-term accuracy
Avoid touching the perforated sensing element directly; skin oils can affect the humidity reading over time
common_mistakes: Reading it faster than once per second, which returns stale or failed (NaN) readings
Wiring VCC/GND backwards
Leaving the code set to DHT22 timing constants when a DHT11 is actually installed

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Serial monitor shows 'Failed to read from DHT sensor'
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Reading too often, loose wiring, or wrong DHTTYPE/DHTPIN defined in code
symptoms_and_causes.check: Confirm DHTTYPE is set to DHT11, add at least a 1-2 second delay between reads, reseat the data wire

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Humidity or temperature always reads the same fixed number
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Sensor is damaged or the DATA line isn't actually connected
symptoms_and_causes.check: Wiggle-test the data wire and verify continuity with a multimeter in continuity mode

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Readings drift or seem off by a few degrees or percent
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Normal DHT11 accuracy limits, or the sensor is near a heat source
symptoms_and_causes.check: Compare against a separate reference thermometer/hygrometer; this may be expected sensor-grade accuracy rather than a fault

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the module powered, measure DC voltage between VCC and GND to confirm 3.5-5.5V is present. The DATA line uses timed pulses rather than a steady voltage, so a multimeter will just show it resting near VCC between reads; an oscilloscope or logic analyzer is needed to see the actual data pulses.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A sensor that measures distance by sending a short click of sound too high to hear and timing the echo, like a bat.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Measuring how far away an object or wall is, for example in an obstacle-avoiding robot or a parking-sensor project.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The Arduino sends the sensor a brief 10-microsecond 'go' pulse on the Trig pin. The sensor then sends 8 pulses of 40 kHz sound (above human hearing) out of one transducer and listens for the echo with the other. It holds the Echo pin high for exactly as long as the round trip took, and the Arduino converts that time into a distance.

pinout.name: VCC
pinout.notes: 5V DC

pinout.name: Trig
pinout.notes: Send a 10us HIGH pulse here to start a measurement

pinout.name: Echo
pinout.notes: Goes HIGH for a duration proportional to distance

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A chip that turns 3 wires from the UNO into 8 separate on/off outputs, so you can control 8 LEDs (or more) without using up 8 of the UNO's own pins.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Driving multiple LEDs or other simple digital loads (like 7-segment displays) from just 3 UNO pins; several 74HC595 chips can be chained together for even more outputs.
function.how_it_works_briefly: You send it 8 bits one at a time on the data pin, pulsing the clock pin each time. Once all 8 bits are in, a pulse on the latch pin copies them all to the 8 output pins at once, so nothing flickers while new data is loading.

pinout.name: GND
pinout.notes: connect to circuit ground

pinout.name: QH'
pinout.notes: carries the overflow bit; connect to the SER pin of the next 74HC595 when chaining chips

pinout.name: SRCLR
pinout.notes: tie HIGH (to VCC) if not used, so the register is never accidentally cleared

pinout.name: SRCLK
pinout.notes: pulse to shift each new data bit in; ELEGOO's own kit tutorial wires this to UNO Digital 9

pinout.name: RCLK
pinout.notes: pulse after 8 bits are shifted in to move them to the outputs; ELEGOO's own kit tutorial wires this to UNO Digital 11

pinout.name: OE
pinout.notes: tie to GND to keep outputs always enabled; can be PWM'd for brightness control

pinout.name: SER
pinout.notes: the incoming data bit stream; ELEGOO's own kit tutorial wires this to UNO Digital 12

pinout.name: VCC
pinout.notes: 2V to 6V supply; typically wired to the UNO's 5V pin

pins.pin_1_identification: With the small U-shaped notch at the top of the chip, pin 1 (QB) is the top-left pin; pin numbers then run counter-clockwise around the package.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A chip that lets a small microcontroller pin safely control a motor that needs more current than the microcontroller can supply, and lets you reverse the motor's direction with software instead of by hand.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Spinning one or two small DC motors (or one stepper motor) forward, backward, or at variable speed using PWM, controlled from UNO digital and PWM pins.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Each of its two independent H-bridges acts like 4 switches arranged around the motor; turning on one diagonal pair of switches drives current one way through the motor, turning on the other diagonal pair reverses it. Built-in diodes absorb the voltage spike that happens whenever a motor is switched off.

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the board powered and a test sketch running, use DC voltage mode to check VCC1 (pin 16) to GND reads about 5V, and VCC2 (pin 8) to GND reads the motor supply voltage. function.what_it_is_used_for: Used as a simple on/off input to the Arduino UNO, for example to trigger an action, count button presses, or start and stop something in a program.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the plastic body, a spring-loaded metal dome sits above two pairs of legs. The two legs on the same side of the switch are always connected to each other, whether pressed or not. Pressing the cap pushes the dome down so it bridges both sides at once, briefly connecting all four legs together. Releasing lifts the dome and breaks that bridge again.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A twist knob that turns how far you turn it into a changing voltage the Arduino can read.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used to make an adjustable analog input, like a volume knob, a brightness dial, or a speed control for something in your program.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the can is a strip of resistive material running end to end, about 10,000 ohms total. A metal wiper contact slides along that strip as you turn the shaft. The pin attached to the wiper picks off whatever fraction of the full 10K it currently sits at, so the voltage on that pin changes smoothly as you turn the knob.

pinout.role: one fixed end of the resistive track

pinout.notes: Wire to an analog input pin such as A0

pinout.role: other fixed end of the resistive track
pinout.notes: Wire to whichever of 5V/GND pin 1 is not using

The pins are evenly spaced (5 mm apart) but unmarked on the part itself.

function.how_it_works_briefly: Seven LED bars (segments a-g) plus one dot (dp) are arranged in the classic figure-8 pattern. This is the common-cathode version, so all 8 LEDs share one ground (cathode) connection. The Arduino lights up whichever segments it needs by sending +5V, through a current-limiting resistor, to each segment pin. Turning on segments a, b, c, d, e, f (but not g) draws a '0', for example.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: Four 7-segment digits in a row, wired so the Arduino lights them one at a time so fast it looks like all four glow at once.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used to show numbers with more than one digit, like a clock, a counter, or a temperature reading with a decimal point.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Each of the 4 digits is a copy of the same 8-LED figure-8 pattern. To save pins, the same 8 segment wires (a-g, dp) are shared by all 4 digits; only one digit's common pin is active at a time (this is the common-anode version, so 'active' means driving that digit's common pin HIGH). The Arduino rapidly cycles through digit 1, 2, 3, 4, showing the right number on each one for a few milliseconds. It happens faster than the eye can see, so it looks like a steady 4-digit number. This trick is called multiplexing.

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set a multimeter to its diode-test function. function.one_sentence_plain_english: A tiny sealed tube with metal balls inside that acts like a switch: closed one way up, open when tilted the other way.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used as a crude orientation or motion sensor, for example to detect if something has been tipped over, shaken, or turned upside down.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the small tube, two tiny conductive balls sit next to two contact pins. Held so the part's own 'upright' side faces down, gravity pulls the balls onto the contacts, closing the circuit. Tilt it far enough the other way (about 10 degrees one direction, about 45 degrees sideways, per the datasheet) and the balls roll away from the contacts, opening the circuit. It is a simple mechanical switch, not an electronic sensor, so it only reports 'past the tilt threshold' or not, never a precise angle.

pinout.name: Lead 1
pinout.role: one side of the internal ball-and-contact switch
pinout.notes: no fixed polarity; interchangeable with lead 2

pinout.name: Lead 2
pinout.role: other side of the internal ball-and-contact switch
pinout.notes: no fixed polarity; interchangeable with lead 1

pins.pin_1_identification: Both leads are electrically identical and interchangeable; there is no 'pin 1' polarity to find. What matters instead is physical orientation: per the manufacturer's diagram, tilting the body so the far (cap) end points down by more than 10 degrees opens the circuit, while tilting so the lead/pin end points down by more than 10 degrees closes it; held on its side, roughly 45 degrees of tilt is needed to change state.

electrical.max_current: not explicitly stated in the fetched manufacturer datasheet; a separate retailer (Sunrom) lists switching current under 5 mA for the same part number
electrical.logic_level: simple dry contact; works fine at 3.3V or 5V logic since it is just a mechanical switch

key_specs.tilt_threshold: about 10 degrees tilting toward the cap or lead end; about 45 degrees tilting sideways (per manufacturer diagram)

visual_identification.color_and_markings: Plain black or gray heat-shrink tube body, no printed text or markings. You can sometimes hear or feel the tiny metal balls rattling faintly inside if you shake it.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: None; the part has no printed label.
easily_confused_with: a small electrolytic capacitor (similar cylindrical shape, but a capacitor is usually shinier or metal-cased and larger, this switch is noticeably shorter and thinner)
a small diode (similar 2-lead axial shape, but a diode is glass or plastic with a printed stripe and part number, this switch is a plain unmarked tube)

example_connections.uno_pin: GND (when using the pin's internal pull-up), or 5V with an external pull-down resistor to the digital pin

required_extra_parts: 10k ohm resistor for an external pull-up/pull-down, or use the UNO's built-in pull-up via pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) and skip the extra resistor
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none needed; read with the built-in digitalRead() function

hazards: none inherent; low voltage, low current, sealed part
handling_notes: do not crush or puncture the tube; it is sealed and not meant to be opened
mounting orientation matters: decide which way is 'up' for the project and test both tilt directions since the switch is not symmetric
common_mistakes: assuming it detects tilt equally in every direction, when per the datasheet it takes only about 10 degrees one way but about 45 degrees the other way or sideways
wiring only one lead, or leaving the input floating without a pull-up/pull-down resistor, causing random readings

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: input never changes no matter how the switch is tilted
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: one lead not actually connected, or the switch is mounted in an orientation where it never crosses its threshold angle
symptoms_and_causes.check: test continuity with a multimeter while manually tilting the part through a full range of angles

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: reading flickers or is unreliable right at the tilt point
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: this is a mechanical ball switch, so near the threshold angle it can bounce between open and closed; this is normal, not a fault
symptoms_and_causes.check: add simple debounce logic in code, or mount it well past the threshold in the intended resting orientation

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to continuity/beep mode and touch a probe to each lead. Slowly rotate the switch through different angles; it should beep (closed) in some orientations and go silent (open) in others, matching the manufacturer's tilt diagram.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small handheld device that sends invisible infrared light signals to remotely control a project, the same way a TV remote works.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Lets a person press buttons to send commands wirelessly to the kit's IR receiver module. The microcontroller reads those commands and reacts, for example changing an LED color or moving a motor, with no wire between the remote and the board.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Pressing a button closes a switch under the remote's rubber keypad. A small chip inside turns that button press into a short burst of blinking infrared light, invisible to the human eye, using the NEC infrared protocol (a widely used on/off blink pattern standard). This is confirmed for the same class of 38 kHz NEC-protocol remote sold with comparable Arduino IR receiver kits; the exact ELEGOO-branded remote was not separately re-tested for protocol this session, but a fetched GitHub example project written specifically for the ELEGOO kit's remote confirms it decodes with the standard IRremote library, which only supports this style of pulse-coded protocol.

Look for a small dark or clear lens at the top edge where the infrared light comes out, and a battery compartment cover on the back that may show a printed plus/minus polarity diagram.

hazards: The internal coin cell battery is a swallowing hazard, especially around young children
A loose coin cell can short and heat up if it touches metal objects like coins or keys in a pocket or drawer
handling_notes: Match the battery's polarity to the marking in the battery compartment when replacing it
Remove the plastic pull-tab insulator before first use if the battery ships pre-installed
Keep the remote out of direct sunlight and high heat, since coin cells and plastic housings degrade faster when hot
common_mistakes: Forgetting to remove the battery insulator tab, so the remote appears dead out of the box
Aiming the remote away from the receiver's sensor window, or standing too far away or at too steep an angle
Assuming the remote works through walls or other solid obstructions; infrared needs a mostly clear line of sight

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: A multimeter cannot read the remote's infrared light output directly. The practical checks are: set a multimeter to DC voltage and touch the probes to the battery contacts inside the compartment to confirm the coin cell still reads close to its rated voltage, and separately, view the remote's infrared lens through a phone camera while pressing a button. Phone camera sensors can usually pick up near-infrared light as a faint flicker that the human eye cannot see, which confirms the remote is transmitting.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A plastic board full of spring-loaded holes that lets you connect electronic parts together temporarily, with no soldering.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Building and testing circuits quickly. You push component legs and wire ends into the holes, and hidden metal clips join the right holes together so current can flow, the same as a soldered connection but removable.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Underneath the plastic top, rows of springy metal clips made of phosphor bronze (a springy copper alloy) grip whatever is pushed into a group of holes and electrically join that whole group into one node. The middle area is organized into short columns of 5 joined holes each. The strips along the top and bottom edges are long rows used to spread power and ground to many parts at once.

pinout.name: 63 columns x 5 holes
pinout.notes: 315 holes. Each column of 5 holes is one electrically joined node, used to plug in a component leg or wire. Not connected to the lower half.

pinout.name: 63 columns x 5 holes
pinout.notes: 315 holes, mirrors the upper half. A center gap running the length of the board separates upper and lower halves; nothing crosses that gap internally.

pinout.name: 2 rows x 50 holes
pinout.notes: 100 holes. One row is marked with a red stripe/plus sign (intended for a positive supply), the other with a blue or black stripe/minus sign (intended for ground). All holes along one marked row are joined into a single long node.

pinout.name: 2 rows x 50 holes
pinout.notes: 100 holes, mirrors the top pair. The top and bottom rail pairs are separate nodes from each other unless a wire bridges them.

pins.pin_1_identification: There is no pin 1. Orientation is read from the printed + and - symbols and red/blue color stripes next to the two power rail rows at the top and bottom edges. A wide unmarked center gap running the long way across the board splits the main circuit area into an upper and lower half that are not connected to each other.

electrical.max_current: 2A per contact point per the manufacturer's rating; real safe current also depends on the gauge of wire plugged in

Two long rows of holes at the very top edge and two at the very bottom edge are marked with a red line and + symbol (one rail of each pair) and a blue or black line and - symbol (the other rail). A wide unmarked gap runs down the center of the board, splitting the main grid into upper and lower halves.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Small printed column numbers along the top of the main hole grid and row letters along one side, silkscreened directly onto the plastic. A peel-off label naming the kit or brand may be stuck to the underside metal backing plate.

hazards: none inherent to the board by itself
a rail can become a shock or fire risk only if a circuit plugged into it exceeds the board's 36V/2A per-contact rating or shorts across a power rail
handling_notes: keep the board dry, the internal spring clips can corrode
do not force oversized leads (thicker than about 0.7 mm, thinner than 21 AWG wire is fine) into the holes, it can permanently spread the internal clips and ruin that hole's grip
peel and stick the metal backing plate to a flat surface if the board needs to stay in place
common_mistakes: assuming the upper and lower halves of the main circuit area are electrically joined across the center gap; they are not
assuming all four power rail rows are tied together; the top pair and bottom pair are usually separate unless bridged with a wire
plugging a component's two legs into what looks like one column but is actually split across the center gap, leaving the circuit open

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: circuit does not work even though the wiring looks right
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: a component leg landed one column off from where a jumper wire is, so they are not actually in the same 5-hole node
symptoms_and_causes.check: recount columns carefully, or test continuity between the two holes with a multimeter

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: intermittent connection, circuit cuts out when the board is bumped
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: a spring clip has worn out after repeated use (rated for about 50,000 insertions) or a lead was too thick or thin for a solid grip
symptoms_and_causes.check: move the same wire to a fresh, unused column and see if the fault follows the wire or stays with that spot on the board

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: part of the circuit has no power
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: assuming the left and right (or top and bottom) power rails are joined together when they are actually separate rail pairs
symptoms_and_causes.check: run a multimeter continuity test along the rail between the point being powered and the point being supplied

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to continuity or resistance mode. Touch one probe to a hole and the other probe to a hole you believe is in the same node (same 5-hole column, or same power rail row). A beep or a reading near 0 ohms confirms they are connected. No beep means they are not connected, or the spring clip has failed.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: This is the cable that plugs the Arduino board into a computer so the computer can power it and load programs onto it.
function.what_it_is_used_for: It connects a computer's USB port to the Arduino UNO board. Through this one cable, the computer both powers the board and sends it a new program (this is called 'uploading a sketch').
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the cable are four wires. Two carry 5 volt power (one wire feeds power in, one is the return path called ground). The other two carry data back and forth as a pair, which is how the computer talks to the tiny chip on the Arduino board that manages the USB connection.

pinout.name: VBUS
pinout.notes: Carries 5 volt power from the computer or USB power adapter to the Arduino board.

pinout.name: D-
pinout.notes: Paired with D+ as a twisted pair inside the cable to carry data while resisting electrical noise.

pinout.name: D+
pinout.notes: Paired with D- as a twisted pair inside the cable to carry data while resisting electrical noise.

pinout.name: GND
pinout.notes: Common return path for both the power and the data signals.

pins.pin_1_identification: There is no separate step to find pin 1 by eye. The connector shells are shaped so the cable only fits one way: the flat, wide end (USB Type-A) plugs into the computer, and the squarish end with slightly rounded top corners (USB Type-B) plugs into the Arduino board. Because the plastic shell is keyed like this, it is physically impossible to insert either end backwards, unlike a battery where you must check + and -.

electrical.operating_voltage: 5V nominal on the VBUS wire, supplied by whatever the Type-A end is plugged into (a computer port or USB power adapter)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: not a separate rating for the cable itself; the voltage is set by the host device's USB port, not by the cable
electrical.typical_current: well under 500 mA for programming and running an Arduino UNO
electrical.max_current: up to 500 mA (the standard USB 2.0 port limit that VBUS is designed to deliver)
electrical.logic_level: not applicable, this is a passive cable and does not process logic signals itself

key_specs.connector_a_end: USB Type-A male (flat, rectangular plug, goes into the computer)
key_specs.connector_b_end: USB Type-B male (squarish plug with two rounded top corners, goes into the Arduino board)
key_specs.example_cable_length: about 3 feet / 1 meter (from a generic retail USB A-B cable, see confidence.notes)

visual_identification.shape_and_size: A cable roughly 3 to 6 feet long with two different plugs on each end. One end is a flat, wide plastic plug (USB Type-A). The other end is a smaller, squarish plug with two gently rounded top corners (USB Type-B).
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Cable jacket is usually black, white, or grey. Connector shells are usually silver-grey metal. No polarity markings are needed because the shape prevents wrong-way insertion.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Cables rarely have printed text; occasionally 'USB 2.0' or 'Hi-Speed' is printed near one of the connectors or on the jacket.
easily_confused_with: USB printer cables (identical Type-A to Type-B shape, this is the same cable style)
USB-A to Micro-USB or USB-A to USB-C cables, which have a much smaller, flatter connector on the device end instead of the squarish Type-B plug

wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none, this is a physical cable; the Arduino IDE handles the USB communication in software

hazards: Low voltage (5V), not a shock hazard under normal use.
Forcing a connector in upside down can bend or break the internal pins if someone tries to force a mismatched or misaligned plug.
handling_notes: Never force the connector; if it does not slide in easily, check you have the right end and the right orientation.
Unplug by pulling the plastic shell, not the cable jacket, to avoid damaging the wires inside.
common_mistakes: Trying to power the board from a phone charge-only cable that lacks the two data wires, which will power the board but prevent uploading a program.
Using a very long or low-quality cable, which can cause upload errors or an unrecognized device.

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Board powers on (lights up) but the computer does not recognize it as a device
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: The cable may be a charge-only cable missing the D+ and D- data wires, or the cable/port is faulty
symptoms_and_causes.check: Try a different, known-good USB A-B cable and a different USB port on the computer

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Uploads fail partway through or are unreliable
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Poor quality or damaged cable, or a bad connection
symptoms_and_causes.check: Reseat both ends firmly, try a shorter cable, and check for a 'device disconnected' message in the computer's device list while wiggling the cable gently

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With one end unplugged, set a multimeter to continuity mode and touch one probe to the VBUS pin (pin 1) on the Type-A end and the other to the VBUS pin on the Type-B end; a beep or near-zero-ohm reading confirms that wire is intact. Repeat for GND (pin 4). The D+ and D- wires are hard to test this way for actual data function, since continuity alone does not prove they carry data correctly.

function.how_it_works_briefly: The wire is solid metal, not stranded, so it holds whatever shape it is bent into. Its bare ends are sized to grip the spring clips hidden inside each breadboard hole, making an electrical connection just by being pushed in.

visual_identification.color_and_markings: Colored plastic insulation (commonly red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, gray, brown, or white) covering most of the wire, with bare, silver-colored metal exposed at both tips. No printed text or labeling on the wire itself.

handling_notes: Bend the wire only at its existing fold. Repeatedly re-bending the same spot fatigues the solid metal and it can snap.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A resistor is a small part that pushes back against electric current (the flow of electricity through a wire), letting less of it through.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Protecting other parts by limiting how much current reaches them, for example placing one in series with an LED so it does not burn out; also used to set voltage levels and as pull-up or pull-down parts in digital circuits.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The resistor's material resists the flow of electrons. Its resistance is measured in Ohms (symbol, the Greek letter Omega). By Ohm's Law (Voltage = Current x Resistance), a higher-value resistor allows less current to flow for a given voltage.

pinout.name: Lead A
pinout.notes: Either lead can connect to either side of the circuit; a resistor has no direction.

pinout.name: Lead B
pinout.notes: Electrically identical to Lead A and interchangeable with it.

pins.pin_1_identification: Not applicable. A resistor has no pin 1 and no positive lead. Both wire leads are electrically identical and can be swapped without changing how the circuit works.

electrical.operating_voltage: Not applicable as a fixed rating. A resistor has no intrinsic operating voltage; it simply limits current per Ohm's Law within whatever voltage the surrounding circuit applies (safe at the Arduino UNO's 5V and 3.3V logic levels).
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: not confirmed for this specific kit's resistors, see confidence notes
electrical.typical_current: Not an intrinsic property; depends on the resistor's value and the circuit voltage (Current = Voltage / Resistance).
electrical.max_current: Limited by the 1/4 W (0.25 watt) power rating; for a given resistance R, the maximum safe current is approximately the square root of (0.25 / R) amps. Exceeding this overheats the part.
electrical.logic_level: not applicable, passive component with no logic output

key_specs.band_code: Standard 4-band color code: band 1 = first digit, band 2 = second digit, band 3 = multiplier (power of ten), band 4 = tolerance (gold = 5%, silver = 10%).

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small light that turns on when current flows through it the correct way, glowing a single color such as red, yellow, green, or blue.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used as a simple visual indicator or status light in a circuit, for example to show that a button was pressed, a sensor was triggered, or a program reached a certain step. In the Arduino starter kit it is one of the first parts used to learn digital output.
function.how_it_works_briefly: An LED is a diode, a part that only lets current flow in one direction. When current flows from the anode (positive lead) to the cathode (negative lead) and the voltage across it reaches the LED's forward voltage (the minimum voltage needed to turn it on), the semiconductor inside emits light. Because an LED's resistance drops sharply once it is lit, it must always be wired in series with a resistor to limit the current, otherwise too much current flows and can damage the LED or the pin driving it.

pinout.name: anode
pinout.notes: The longer of the two leads on a new, untrimmed LED.

pinout.name: cathode
pinout.role: negative terminal, current exits here (to ground)
pinout.notes: The shorter lead. Also marked by a flat-ground spot on the rim of the plastic dome on the same side as this lead, useful once leads have been trimmed or bent.

pins.pin_1_identification: Hold the LED with both leads visible: the longer lead is the anode (positive). If the leads have been trimmed to equal length, look instead for a flat spot ground into the rim of the clear plastic dome; the lead closest to that flat side is the cathode (negative).

electrical.operating_voltage: Forward voltage depends on color. A simpler reference from Adafruit's equivalent diffused 5mm LED pack states approximately 2.0V for red/yellow/green and approximately 3.3V for blue/white, both at 20mA. Treat red/yellow/green as roughly 2V and blue/white as roughly 3.3V for quick series-resistor math.

hazards: Very low voltage and current, not a shock or fire hazard under normal use
Driving the LED without a series resistor lets too much current flow, which can burn out the LED almost instantly and can also damage the Arduino pin driving it

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to diode-test mode (the diode symbol). Touch the red probe to the anode (long lead) and the black probe to the cathode (short lead / flat-side lead); a healthy LED will glow faintly and the display will show a forward voltage drop reading (commonly in the 1.6V to 3.6V range depending on color). Swapping the probes should show no reading (open circuit) in the reverse direction, which confirms the part behaves as a diode rather than being shorted or open.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A single LED bulb that has three tiny colored lights, red, green, and blue, built into one clear or frosted dome, so one part can glow almost any color.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used in Arduino projects to create custom multi-colored or animated lighting effects, such as mood lighting, status indicators, or simple color displays, using one component instead of three separate single-color LEDs.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the dome are three separate tiny LED chips, one red, one green, one blue, that all share one common ground leg (this part is the common cathode type, meaning that shared leg is the negative side). Sending a rapidly pulsing signal (PWM, or pulse width modulation) of different average brightness to each of the three color legs mixes the light your eye sees into a wide range of colors, similar to how a TV or phone screen mixes red, green, and blue dots.

symptoms_and_causes.check: Verify the longest leg goes to GND, move it there if it was on 5V

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Only some colors light up
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: A resistor or jumper wire is missing or loose on one or more color legs, or that pin is not being driven in the sketch
symptoms_and_causes.check: Use a multimeter to check continuity from the Arduino pin through the resistor to the LED leg, and confirm the sketch writes to that pin

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Colors look dim or washed out
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Resistor value is too high, or the PWM duty cycle in the sketch is too low
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure voltage across the LED leg while PWM is active, and compare the resistor's value to the typical 220 ohm reference

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: One color is noticeably dimmer than the others at the same PWM level
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Different color dies have different forward voltages, red is lower than green or blue, so identical resistors make red appear brighter or dimmer than the others depending on wiring
symptoms_and_causes.check: This can be normal behavior, try a different resistor value on the mismatched color leg to balance perceived brightness

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to diode-test mode. Put the black (COM) probe on the longest leg (the common cathode) and touch the red probe to each of the other three legs in turn. Each color die should light dimly and the meter should show a forward-voltage-like reading, red typically the lowest, green and blue typically similar and a bit higher. If a color die does not light during this test, that die is likely damaged or that leg was misidentified.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small two-wire part whose electrical resistance changes with temperature, so Arduino can measure temperature by measuring resistance.
function.what_it_is_used_for: In this kit it is used for the temperature-sensing lesson, for example a simple thermometer readout or a temperature-triggered project such as a fan that turns on when it gets warm, read through one analog input pin on the Arduino.
function.how_it_works_briefly: It is an NTC (negative temperature coefficient) resistor, meaning its resistance goes down as temperature goes up. Paired with a fixed resistor (commonly 10k ohm) to form a voltage divider, the voltage at the midpoint of the two resistors changes with temperature. Arduino reads that voltage on an analog pin with analogRead(), then a formula in the code (often called the Beta equation) converts the reading into a temperature.

a photoresistor (LDR), but a photoresistor has a flat top with a visible zig-zag light-sensing surface, while this part is a smooth solid blob with no visible sensing pattern

wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none required, read with the built-in analogRead() function and convert to temperature using the Beta equation in the sketch's own code

hazards: No electric shock risk at Arduino's low 5V
very high external heat can crack or melt the epoxy bead
handling_notes: the two wire leads are thin and can fatigue or break if bent back and forth at the same spot
no polarity, so it cannot be plugged in backwards
avoid pushing more than a few mA through it, extra current causes self-heating that makes the reading inaccurate
common_mistakes: wiring it alone without the companion fixed resistor, so the analog pin just reads a fixed rail voltage instead of a changing one
using a B-value or resistor value in the code's formula that does not match the one actually wired in, which throws off the computed temperature
mistaking it for a photoresistor since both are small unlabeled two-lead sensors

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: analog reading is stuck near the top (about 1023) or bottom (about 0)
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: missing the companion divider resistor, or a broken or loose connection
symptoms_and_causes.check: confirm a fixed resistor completes the voltage divider and both leads are firmly connected

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: temperature reading is wildly wrong or does not change at all
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: wrong B-value or divider-resistor value used in the sketch's formula, or a bad connection
symptoms_and_causes.check: measure the resistance across the two leads directly with a multimeter and compare to the expected 10k ohm at room temperature

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: reading slowly climbs while the circuit sits untouched
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: self-heating from too much current flowing through the thermistor
symptoms_and_causes.check: measure the divider current, and increase the fixed resistor value or reduce supply voltage if the current is too high

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Disconnect the thermistor from the circuit, set the multimeter to resistance (ohms) mode, and measure across its two leads. At room temperature, about 25 C, expect roughly 10,000 ohms. Warm the bead slightly, for example by holding it between two fingers, and the reading should drop. Let it cool and the reading should rise again, confirming normal NTC behavior.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A diode is a one-way valve for electric current: it lets current flow easily in one direction, from the anode to the cathode, and blocks it in the other direction.
function.what_it_is_used_for: In this kit it is mainly used as a flyback diode, also called a freewheeling diode, wired backwards across a relay coil or motor. Coils and motors are inductive loads, meaning that when the current driving them is suddenly switched off, the collapsing magnetic field creates a brief high-voltage spike in the opposite direction. The diode sits reverse-biased (blocking, doing nothing) during normal operation, but that voltage spike forward-biases it for an instant, giving the spike a safe path to dissipate instead of destroying the transistor or Arduino pin that was driving the coil. The same part can also rectify, meaning convert AC to pulsing DC, in a basic power supply, though that is not how this kit's tutorial uses it.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the diode is a P-N junction, the boundary between two differently-doped regions of silicon. When the anode side is at a higher voltage than the cathode side, the junction conducts and current flows easily with roughly a 0.7 to 1.1 volt drop across it. When the voltage is reversed, the junction blocks current, up to the diode's rated reverse voltage of 1000V, beyond which it can break down and fail.

pinout.name: Cathode
pinout.role: Current exits here during forward conduction. This is the terminal marked by the painted stripe/band on the body.
pinout.notes: In flyback wiring across a coil, this lead connects toward the positive/supply side of the coil so the diode stays reverse-biased in normal operation.

pinout.name: Anode
pinout.role: Current enters here during forward conduction. This is the unmarked end, with no stripe.
pinout.notes: In flyback wiring, this lead connects to the switched node, for example the collector of the transistor or relay driver that pulls the coil low.

pins.pin_1_identification: Look for the single light-colored stripe or band painted around the body near one end. The lead closest to that stripe is the cathode. This is a bare through-hole part, not a module, so there is no printed pin-1 marker other than the stripe.

electrical.operating_voltage: Not a powered/logic part. When forward-biased (conducting) it drops about 0.93V typical (1.1V max) at 1A. When reverse-biased it blocks voltage up to its rated maximum (see absolute_max_voltage).
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: 1000V VRRM (peak repetitive reverse voltage); 1200V VRSM (non-repetitive surge reverse voltage, half-wave single-phase 60Hz); 700V VR(RMS).
electrical.typical_current: Up to 1.0A average rectified forward current (IO), single-phase resistive load, 60Hz, 75 degrees C ambient.
electrical.max_current: 30A non-repetitive peak surge current (IFSM) for one 8.3ms half-cycle (60Hz surge rating). Continuous current above 1.0A average is outside the rated spec.
electrical.logic_level: not_applicable

key_specs.package_case: DO-41 outline (onsemi Case 59-10), axial-lead, epoxy molded, about 0.4 gram
key_specs.VF_forward_voltage_drop: 0.93 V typical, 1.1 V max, at 1.0A forward current, 25 C junction temperature
key_specs.IR_reverse_leakage_current: 10 uA max at 25 C junction temp; 50 uA max at 100 C junction temp
key_specs.body_dimensions: 4.10 to 5.20 mm long, 2.00 to 2.70 mm diameter (0.161 to 0.205 in by 0.079 to 0.106 in)

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Small cylindrical body about 5.2mm long and 2.7mm in diameter, roughly the size of a grain of rice, with two thin wire leads extending straight out from each end (each at least 25mm long before any bend).
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Solid black or dark gray epoxy body with a single light gray or white stripe/band painted near one end. That band marks the cathode lead.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: 1N4007 printed in small white or gray text along the body. Some units also show a date code (year and work week) and a small manufacturer logo.
easily_confused_with: 1N4001 through 1N4006 (identical black cylindrical body and stripe marking, differ only in the printed number and reverse-voltage rating)
1N4148 / 1N914 small-signal switching diode (similar stripe marking but a much smaller clear glass body, not black plastic, and cannot handle 1A)
Zener diodes in the same DO-41 package (look externally identical, only the printed part number and a datasheet lookup tell them apart)

example_connections.uno_pin: Not wired to an Arduino pin directly. Connects to the positive/supply-side terminal of the relay coil or motor (the same node as the coil's Vcc / flyback supply connection).

Not wired to an Arduino pin directly. Connects to the switched node, i.e. the relay driver transistor's collector or the motor driver output, so the diode is reverse-biased during normal operation and only conducts during the coil's turn-off voltage spike.

required_extra_parts: Relay module or DC motor (the inductive load the diode protects)
NPN transistor or MOSFET driving the coil, if building a discrete driver instead of using a relay module
External power supply appropriate for the relay/motor coil
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none. The diode is a passive protection component; it is not addressed by Arduino code.

hazards: Not a shock or fire hazard by itself at hobby voltages, but if installed backwards (reversed polarity) across an inductive load, it will not block the flyback voltage spike, letting that spike damage the driving transistor or an Arduino pin.
If driven well beyond its 1A / 1000V ratings, for example wired directly across a live AC mains circuit without a current-limiting load, it can overheat and rupture.
handling_notes: Do not bend the leads sharply right at the body. Bend at least a few millimeters away from the body to avoid cracking the glass-passivated junction inside.
Leads conduct soldering heat toward the body. Avoid holding a lead near the body for more than a few seconds while soldering.
common_mistakes: Installing the diode with the stripe (cathode) on the wrong side, which reverses its polarity and defeats its job as a flyback diode.
Leaving the flyback diode out entirely across a relay coil or motor, letting inductive voltage spikes reach and potentially damage the driving transistor or Arduino pin.
Confusing it with a similarly shaped small-signal diode, such as a 1N4148, which cannot handle 1A of current.

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Relay driver transistor (or motor driver IC) fails repeatedly after a period of use
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Missing flyback diode, or diode installed backwards, so the coil's turn-off voltage spike is not being clamped
symptoms_and_causes.check: Visually confirm the diode is present across the coil with the cathode stripe toward the supply/positive side. Verify polarity with a multimeter diode test.

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Diode measures as an open circuit in both directions
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Diode has failed open, usually from an excessive voltage spike or current surge
symptoms_and_causes.check: Multimeter diode test in both directions. A good diode reads roughly 0.5 to 0.8V one way and open (OL) the other.

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Diode measures as a short circuit in both directions
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Junction failure from overcurrent or reverse-voltage breakdown
symptoms_and_causes.check: Multimeter diode test. If shorted, replace the part, and check the upstream circuit for whatever caused the overcurrent or overvoltage before powering back up.

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to diode test mode (the diode symbol). Touch the red lead to the anode (unstriped end) and the black lead to the cathode (striped end): a good diode shows roughly 0.5 to 0.8V forward voltage drop. Reverse the leads: a good diode shows an open circuit (OL). If both directions read near 0V, the diode is shorted; if both read OL, it is open, either way it needs replacing.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: It is a small light sensor whose resistance drops as the light around it gets brighter, so an Arduino can read it to tell how bright or dark a room is.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Sensing ambient light level for projects like automatic night lights, light-triggered alarms, or dimming controls. It is wired into a voltage divider (a pair of resistors that splits a voltage) so the changing resistance turns into a changing voltage that the Arduino can measure.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The disc is coated with cadmium sulfide (CdS), a material whose electrical resistance falls when more light hits it. In the dark its resistance is very high (over 1 megaohm, meaning 1,000,000 ohms), and in typical room-level light (defined as 10 lux, a unit of light brightness) it drops to roughly 8,000 to 20,000 ohms for this part. Paired with a second, fixed resistor, it forms a voltage divider whose midpoint voltage rises and falls with light level, and the Arduino reads that voltage with analogRead().

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: the reading moves opposite to what the code expects (goes down in bright light instead of up, or vice versa)
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: the divider is wired with the photoresistor on the opposite leg from what the sketch assumes
symptoms_and_causes.check: trace which lead goes toward 5V and which goes toward GND/A0, and match that to the sketch's logic

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: reading is stuck near 0 or near the maximum value regardless of light
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: a short or open circuit in the sensor itself or its partner resistor
symptoms_and_causes.check: disconnect the sensor and measure resistance directly across its two leads in bright light and then fully covered

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to resistance (ohms) mode and measure directly across the two leads with the part disconnected from the circuit (or at least isolated). Under normal indoor room light, expect roughly 8 to 20 kOhm (thousands of ohms) for this part at a moderate 10 lux brightness. Fully cover the disc so no light reaches it, and the reading should climb to over 1 MOhm (millions of ohms).
