function.one_sentence_plain_english: A tiny electronic switch that lets a weak signal from the Arduino turn a bigger current on or off.
function.what_it_is_used_for: In this kit it is used to let a small 5V signal from the UNO control something that needs more current than an Arduino pin can safely supply, such as a relay coil or a small motor. It can also amplify a weak signal.
function.how_it_works_briefly: It is an NPN bipolar transistor with three legs: base, collector, and emitter. A small current flowing into the base lets a much larger current flow from the collector to the emitter, acting like a switch controlled by voltage.

pinout.name: E
pinout.notes: Usually wired toward ground (ground side of the load path).

pinout.name: B
pinout.notes: The control input. Drive this from an Arduino pin through a series resistor (about 1k Ohm), never straight from the pin.

pinout.name: C
pinout.notes: Usually wired to the negative side of the load being switched.

pins.pin_1_identification: Hold the transistor with the flat printed face toward you and the three wire legs pointing down. Reading left to right in that orientation, the legs are Emitter, Base, Collector (E-B-C), per the onsemi/Fairchild datasheet's TO-92 pin diagram.

electrical.operating_voltage: Not self-powered; it switches whatever voltage the load circuit uses, up to its maximum ratings below. The base can be driven directly from a 5V Arduino digital pin through a base resistor.
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: Collector-Emitter (VCEO): 40V. Collector-Base (VCBO): 75V. Emitter-Base (VEBO): 6.0V.
electrical.typical_current: Datasheet describes it as suited for medium-power switching and amplifying up to about 500 mA of collector current in typical use.
electrical.max_current: 1.0 A absolute maximum collector current (IC).
electrical.logic_level: Base-emitter turn-on voltage is roughly 0.6-0.7V, compatible with a 5V logic HIGH from an Arduino digital pin through a base resistor.

key_specs.dc_current_gain_hFE: Ranges from 35 to 300 depending on collector current and test conditions (e.g. hFE is at least 100 at IC=150mA, VCE=10V)
key_specs.max_power_dissipation: 625 mW at 25C ambient, derated 5.0 mW per additional degree C
key_specs.collector_emitter_saturation_voltage: 0.3V typical at IC=150mA, IB=15mA (rises to 1.0V at IC=500mA, IB=50mA)

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Small black plastic part shaped like a half-cylinder, roughly 5mm wide and 5mm tall (TO-92 package), with a flat face on one side and a rounded back, and three thin wire legs coming straight down from the bottom in a single row spaced about 1.27mm apart.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Solid black (sometimes dark grey) plastic body. The part number is usually printed in small light-colored text on the flat face.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: PN2222A (sometimes shortened to PN2222 or shown as an equivalent like 2N2222) printed on the flat side of the case.
easily_confused_with: Other TO-92 transistors such as the 2N3904 or 2N2222, which look visually identical; the printed part number is the only reliable way to tell them apart
Small 3-terminal voltage regulators, which use the same black TO-92-style body

example_connections.uno_pin: A digital output pin (e.g. D9) through a series base resistor of about 1k Ohm
Not connected directly to the UNO; wired to the negative/return side of the load being switched (for example, a relay coil or small motor), with the load's other side going to the external supply

required_extra_parts: A base resistor, about 1k Ohm, in series between the Arduino pin and the base
A flyback diode (such as the kit's 1N4007) placed across any inductive load like a relay coil or motor to protect the transistor
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none; controlled directly with digitalWrite() or analogWrite() on the pin driving the base resistor

hazards: Wiring the collector and emitter reversed, or connecting the base directly to 5V without a resistor, can overheat and permanently damage the transistor
Switching an inductive load such as a motor or relay coil without a flyback diode across it can produce a voltage spike large enough to destroy the transistor
handling_notes: Bend the leads gently and well away from the plastic body; bending right where the lead meets the body can crack the internal seal
The three leads are close together, so check for solder bridges after soldering
common_mistakes: Treating it like a simple on/off switch and skipping the base resistor
Mixing up the base and collector legs since all three leads look identical
Confusing an NPN part like this one with a PNP part, which is wired the opposite way

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: The load never turns on
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Base resistor value too high, base wired to the wrong pin, or a bad connection
symptoms_and_causes.check: With the Arduino pin driven HIGH, measure the voltage at the base leg relative to the emitter; it should read about 0.6 to 0.7V

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: The transistor gets hot or smells burnt
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Missing base resistor, reversed collector/emitter wiring, or a missing flyback diode on an inductive load
symptoms_and_causes.check: Power off immediately, let it cool, and recheck the wiring against the E-B-C pinout before reapplying power

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: The load stays on all the time even when the Arduino pin is LOW
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Collector and emitter leads swapped, or a solder bridge shorting two legs together
symptoms_and_causes.check: Visually inspect solder joints and confirm each leg lands in the correct breadboard row

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to diode-test mode. Touch the red probe to the base and the black probe to the emitter, then to the collector; each should show a diode-like forward drop of about 0.5 to 0.7V. Reverse the probes and both readings should show open circuit (OL). This confirms two working NPN junctions from the base.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: This is a small circuit board that senses how it is tilted, how fast it is spinning, and how fast it is accelerating in any direction.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used in projects that need to know orientation or motion, like self-balancing robots, drones, and tilt-controlled games.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The chip contains a tiny mechanical structure (called MEMS) for sensing acceleration and another for sensing rotation. Both sensor types are built into one chip, and it reports the readings to the Arduino over a two-wire I2C connection.

pinout.name: VCC
pinout.notes: Module power input. On the bare MPU-6050 chip this maps to the VDD pin (chip pin 13), which needs 2.375-3.46V; this breakout is commonly wired straight to a 5V Arduino pin by sellers, but a module-level regulator or level shift was not independently confirmed from a fetched source.

pinout.name: GND
pinout.notes: Maps to the chip's GND pin (chip pin 18).

pinout.name: SCL
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's analog pin 5 (SCL), per ELEGOO's own tutorial. Maps to the chip's SCL pin (chip pin 23).

pinout.name: SDA
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's analog pin 4 (SDA), per ELEGOO's own tutorial. Maps to the chip's SDA pin (chip pin 24).

pinout.name: XDA
pinout.notes: Maps to the chip's AUX_DA pin (chip pin 6). Lets the MPU-6050 act as an I2C master to a second sensor, like an external magnetometer. Leave unconnected for basic accelerometer/gyro use.

pinout.name: XCL
pinout.notes: Maps to the chip's AUX_CL pin (chip pin 7). Pairs with XDA above. Leave unconnected for basic use.

pinout.name: AD0
pinout.notes: Maps to the chip's AD0 pin (chip pin 9). Leave unconnected or tie low for I2C address 0x68 (default); tie high for 0x69, useful when two of these modules share a bus.

pinout.name: INT
pinout.notes: Maps to the chip's INT pin (chip pin 12). Goes high (or low, depending on configuration) when new sensor data is ready, if enabled in software. Optional for basic polling use.

pins.pin_1_identification: No numbered pin 1. Find the single row of 8 pin holes along one edge of the board, printed left to right VCC GND SCL SDA XDA XCL AD0 INT on the standard GY-521 breakout silkscreen. The small square sensor chip sits near the center of the board, often mounted at a slight diagonal angle.

electrical.operating_voltage: Bare MPU-6050 chip: VDD 2.375V-3.46V (InvenSense/TDK Product Specification Rev 3.4). Module-level input voltage as wired by sellers is commonly described as 3-5V tolerant thanks to an onboard regulator, but this was not independently confirmed from a fetched source for this specific board.
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: -0.5V to +6V on the VDD pin, and -0.5V to VDD+0.5V on VLOGIC and the digital I/O pins (InvenSense/TDK Product Specification Rev 3.4, bare chip). Module-level absolute maximum not independently confirmed.
electrical.typical_current: 3.9 mA with gyroscope, accelerometer, and Digital Motion Processor (DMP) all enabled; 3.8 mA with DMP disabled (InvenSense/TDK Product Specification Rev 3.4, bare chip)
electrical.max_current: not confirmed beyond the typical operating-current figures above; no explicit maximum current spec was found in the fetched datasheet's electrical tables
electrical.logic_level: VLOGIC reference is 1.71V to VDD on the bare chip (InvenSense/TDK datasheet); this breakout module commonly ties VLOGIC internally to its own VCC per typical GY-521 board design, which was not independently confirmed from a fetched source

key_specs.sensor_type: 6-axis: 3-axis MEMS gyroscope + 3-axis MEMS accelerometer, plus an onboard temperature sensor (InvenSense/TDK datasheet)
key_specs.adc_resolution: 16-bit for both the gyroscope and accelerometer channels (InvenSense/TDK datasheet)
key_specs.i2c_address: 0x68 with AD0 pin low (default), 0x69 with AD0 pin high (InvenSense/TDK datasheet)
key_specs.onboard_dmp: Yes on the true MPU-6050 (Digital Motion Processor does sensor fusion in hardware); not confirmed whether the alternate QMI8658 chip mentioned in ELEGOO's tutorial has an equivalent feature

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Small rectangular PCB, about 2.1 cm x 1.6 cm, with a single row of 8 pin holes along one long edge.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Commonly sold with a blue PCB; exact color as bundled in this specific ELEGOO kit was not independently confirmed from a fetched photo source. A small square chip (roughly 4mm x 4mm) sits near the center of the board, often mounted at a slight diagonal.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: "GY-521" printed on the board silkscreen, plus pin labels VCC GND SCL SDA XDA XCL AD0 INT along the header edge. Check the tiny text printed on the chip itself to tell an MPU-6050 apart from a QMI8658.
easily_confused_with: Other small blue I2C breakout boards of similar size (for example a BMP280 barometric pressure breakout)
GY-521 boards built around a QMI8658 chip instead of an MPU-6050 (identical board silkscreen and pin labels, different chip inside)

required_extra_parts: 4 female-to-male Dupont wires (per ELEGOO's own kit tutorial)
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: ELEGOO's tutorial calls for installing a library it labels "GY-521"; commonly this is fulfilled by an MPU6050 library such as the one from Jeff Rowberg's I2Cdevlib or Electronic Cats

hazards: Reversing VCC and GND can damage the chip
Static discharge can damage the exposed I2C header pins
handling_notes: Handle the board by its edges
Double-check wire orientation against the printed pin labels before powering on
common_mistakes: Wiring SDA and SCL swapped
Assuming a 5V-safe onboard regulator without checking, since the bare chip itself only tolerates up to 3.46V on VDD

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: I2C device not found
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Wrong I2C address, or SDA/SCL swapped
symptoms_and_causes.check: Run an I2C scanner sketch; expect to see address 0x68 (or 0x69 if AD0 is tied high)

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Garbage or noisy readings
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Loose Dupont wiring or vibration during a reading
symptoms_and_causes.check: Reseat all wires and hold the sensor still while checking baseline values

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With power applied, measure between the VCC and GND pins; expect a reading close to the supply voltage you wired in (commonly 5V from the Uno). A multimeter cannot verify I2C communication; use an I2C scanner sketch for that.

components.mpn: DS1307, named directly in ELEGOO's own kit tutorial (both the lesson prose and the required code library are called "DS1307"). However, the same tutorial's wiring instructions describe a 6-pin header and say to "ignore the 32K and SQW pins." The genuine DS1307 chip (per its Dallas/Analog Devices datasheet) has no separate 32K output pin, only a combined SQW/OUT pin; a board with both a 32K pin and a SQW pin is the standard pinout for a DS3231-based module. This is an unresolved contradiction between ELEGOO's own descriptive text and its own wiring diagram. We could not confirm from a fetched source which chip is actually populated on kits shipping today.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: This module keeps track of the date and time, even when the Arduino is turned off, thanks to a small backup battery.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Used any time a project needs to know or display the current date and time, such as a clock, a data logger that timestamps readings, or an alarm.
function.how_it_works_briefly: A dedicated timekeeping chip counts seconds, minutes, hours, days, months, and years using its own crystal oscillator, and reports them to the Arduino over I2C. A small coin-cell battery keeps it running even when the Arduino's main power is unplugged.

pinout.name: 32K
pinout.notes: 32.768 kHz square wave output pin, left unused in ELEGOO's tutorial wiring. This pin is documented for DS3231-family RTC chips; its presence on a board ELEGOO's tutorial text calls a "DS1307" module is part of why the true chip is uncertain here (see confidence notes).

pinout.name: SQW
pinout.notes: Programmable square-wave or interrupt output, left unused in ELEGOO's basic tutorial wiring. Open-drain and needs an external pull-up on the real DS1307 chip (per the DS1307 datasheet).

pinout.name: SCL
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's SCL pin (analog pin 5), per ELEGOO's own tutorial.

pinout.name: SDA
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's SDA pin (analog pin 4), per ELEGOO's own tutorial. Open-drain and needs an external pull-up resistor (per the DS1307 datasheet); most breakout boards include this pull-up onboard.

pinout.name: VCC
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's 5V pin, per ELEGOO's own tutorial. The DS1307 chip itself requires 4.5V to 5.5V (DS1307 datasheet), so this module is 5V only, not confirmed safe on 3.3V logic.

pinout.name: GND
pinout.notes: Wire to the Arduino Uno's GND pin.

pins.pin_1_identification: No numbered pin 1. The six pins are printed left to right on the header as 32K, SQW, SCL, SDA, VCC, GND, per ELEGOO's own tutorial wiring diagram. A round coin-cell battery holder on the board is the other clear identifying feature.

electrical.operating_voltage: 5V (DS1307 datasheet: VCC 4.5V to 5.5V; this module is not confirmed safe on a 3.3V logic board)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: -0.5V to +7.0V on any pin relative to ground (DS1307 datasheet, Dallas Semiconductor/Analog Devices)
electrical.typical_current: up to 1.5 mA active supply current at 100 kHz SCL clocking (DS1307 datasheet); 300 nA typical battery-backup current at 25 degrees C with the oscillator running and SQW/OUT off (DS1307 datasheet)
electrical.max_current: 1.5 mA active supply current maximum, 200 microamp standby current maximum, 500 nA battery-backup current maximum at 25 degrees C (DS1307 datasheet)
electrical.logic_level: 5V; the SDA and SQW/OUT pins are open-drain and need an external pull-up, which is normally already present on the breakout board (DS1307 datasheet)

key_specs.timekeeping_fields: seconds, minutes, hours, day of week, date, month, year, with automatic leap-year correction valid through the year 2100 (DS1307 datasheet)
key_specs.backup_ram: 56 bytes of battery-backed nonvolatile RAM built into the DS1307 chip (DS1307 datasheet)
key_specs.oscillator: external 32.768 kHz quartz crystal, 12.5 pF load capacitance (DS1307 datasheet)

confidence.notes: Seed data guessed "DS3231 (older kits DS1307)". ELEGOO's own official tutorial PDF for this exact kit (Lesson 19, Real Time Clock Module) names the part DS1307 in both its prose and its required code library, which runs opposite to the seed's guess. But the same tutorial's own wiring section instructs the reader to "ignore the 32K and SQW pins," describing a 6-pin header (32K, SQW, SCL, SDA, VCC, GND). The genuine DS1307 chip has no 32K pin per its datasheet; only the DS3231 family does. Both chips are commonly sold on an identical generic 6-pin breakout PCB (often called a "Tiny RTC" board), with the populated chip swapped between production runs depending on cost and availability, and only the tiny printed part number on the chip itself differing. The most reliable way to settle this for a given physical unit is to read that printed part number directly off the black 8-pin chip on the board.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: This sensor tells you roughly how deep it is submerged in water, by measuring how many of its exposed copper strips are touching the water.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Detecting rainfall, measuring water depth in a container, or building a simple water-leak alarm.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The sensor has a comb of exposed parallel copper traces. Water bridges neighboring traces and lowers the resistance between them; a small onboard transistor amplifier converts that changing resistance into an analog voltage the Arduino can read. The higher the water rises up the comb, the more traces get bridged and the higher the output voltage.

hazards: Submerging anything beyond the marked copper comb area (the header or wiring) risks short circuits or long-term corrosion
Standing water near mains-powered equipment is an electrical hazard in general, though this sensor itself only runs on a safe low voltage (5V)
handling_notes: Dry the sensor thoroughly after use to slow corrosion of the exposed copper traces
Do not exceed the rated voltage

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Wiring fault, or water not reaching high enough up the comb
symptoms_and_causes.check: Confirm + and - are wired correctly, then wet more of the comb and watch the reading change

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Reading drifts over repeated use
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Corrosion building up on the copper traces from repeated wetting
symptoms_and_causes.check: Gently clean the copper traces and compare a fresh dry-air reading against the original baseline

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the board powered, measure the S pin's voltage relative to GND while dry (expect it near 0V) and again with the comb dipped in water (expect it to rise); this confirms the sensor's analog behavior even without a microcontroller attached.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small board with a tiny microphone that tells the Arduino how loud the sound around it is, and can also just say yes or no once it gets loud enough.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Detecting sound or loudness, for example a clap-activated switch, a noise alarm, or any sound-triggered project.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The microphone turns sound into a tiny voltage. An onboard amplifier boosts that signal, which comes out on the AO (analog output) pin as a continuously changing voltage. A comparator circuit (a chip that checks whether one voltage is bigger than another) compares the amplified signal to a threshold set by the blue trimmer potentiometer (a small adjustable resistor you turn with a screwdriver); when the sound crosses that threshold, the DO (digital output) pin flips between high and low.

function.what_it_is_used_for: User input, for example a door lock code pad, a simple calculator, or menu navigation.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The 16 keys are wired in a grid of 4 rows and 4 columns, so only 8 wires are needed instead of 16. Under each key is a simple switch that, when pressed, connects one row wire to one column wire. The Arduino repeatedly checks each row and column combination (a process called scanning) to work out which single key was pressed.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A sensor that notices when a warm, moving body like a person walks nearby, the same basic idea as a security light's motion detector.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Motion-activated lights, alarms, or any project that should react when someone walks by.
function.how_it_works_briefly: The sensor has two halves, each of which senses a little bit of the infrared heat coming from the room. When a warm body passes by, it changes the heat hitting one half before the other, creating a brief difference between them. The onboard circuit turns that difference into a simple high signal on the output pin.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A tiny capacitor that stores a very small electric charge and is almost always used in a matched pair to help a quartz crystal start up and keep steady time.
function.what_it_is_used_for: This kit does not wire it into a single named lesson by itself. Its standard job, and the reason it is bundled at all, is as a load capacitor on the two legs of a quartz crystal on a microcontroller. The ATmega328 datasheet lists 12-22 pF as its recommended crystal load capacitor range, which is why kits built around the ATmega328 (the chip on the UNO) include 22pF capacitors.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Two conductive plates separated by a ceramic insulator. It charges and discharges almost instantly, far faster than an electrolytic capacitor, which is exactly the behavior a crystal oscillator circuit needs: two of these capacitors, one from each crystal leg to ground, present a combined load capacitance that lets the crystal oscillate at its rated frequency.

common_mistakes: confusing it with the visually similar 104 capacitor since both are small ceramic discs

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to capacitance mode (the F or farad symbol) and clip the probes to the two leads; expect a reading close to 22 pF. Many basic multimeters only resolve down to nF or pF ranges with reduced accuracy at this small a value, so treat the reading as approximate.

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small capacitor that soaks up tiny, fast voltage bumps on a power line, usually placed right next to the chip that needs clean power.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Commonly called a decoupling or bypass capacitor. Placed as close as possible to the power pins of a chip, such as the ATmega328 on the UNO or any IC added on the breadboard, to absorb quick voltage spikes and switching noise so the chip runs reliably.
function.how_it_works_briefly: It is a small reservoir of charge that reacts almost instantly, much faster than a battery or a larger electrolytic capacitor. When a chip suddenly needs a brief burst of current, this capacitor supplies it locally instead of forcing the current to travel all the way back from the main power supply, which reduces noise and voltage dips.

pinout.notes: Either lead can connect to either side of the circuit; no polarity.

pinout.name: Lead B
pinout.notes: Electrically identical to Lead A and interchangeable with it.

pins.pin_1_identification: Not applicable. There is no positive lead. Both leads are electrically identical and can be swapped without changing the circuit.

key_specs.marking_code: Printed as '104': the first two digits (10) are the significant figures, and the third digit (4) is the power-of-ten multiplier in picofarads, so 10 x 10^4 pF = 100,000 pF = 100 nF.

visual_identification.shape_and_size: A small flat disc, slightly larger than the 22pF part, roughly 5-7 mm across, with two straight wire leads about 0.1 inch apart.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Body color varies by supplier, commonly blue or yellow/tan. Printed with '104'.
easily_confused_with: 22pF ceramic capacitor: same disc shape but marked '22' instead of '104' and usually a visibly smaller body
other 3-digit-coded ceramic capacitors such as 103 (10 nF) or 105 (1 uF), distinguished only by the printed number

example_connections.uno_pin: 5V or a chip's power pin, wired as close to the chip as possible
GND, forming a short path directly across the chip's power and ground pins

wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none

hazards: none under normal use within its 50V rating
handling_notes: no polarity to worry about
keep lead lengths short when using it as a decoupling capacitor; long leads add inductance that reduces how well it filters fast noise
common_mistakes: confusing it with the visually similar 22pF capacitor since both are small ceramic discs
expecting it to smooth slow, large power dips the way a bigger electrolytic capacitor does; 100 nF only helps with fast, high-frequency noise

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: a chip resets randomly, glitches, or misbehaves only under load
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: missing decoupling capacitor, or one placed too far from the chip's power pins
symptoms_and_causes.check: confirm a 104 capacitor sits close to the chip's power pins; measure with a multimeter's capacitance mode and expect a reading close to 100 nF (often shown as 0.10 on a uF-range meter)

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to capacitance mode and read across the two leads; expect roughly 100 nF (0.1 uF).

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small can-shaped capacitor that stores much more charge than a ceramic capacitor and smooths out slower power dips, but only works if wired the correct way around.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Filtering and smoothing power-supply ripple or voltage dips, for example after a voltage regulator or near a part that pulls current in short bursts.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Like the ceramic capacitors in this kit, it stores charge on two plates, but the plates are rolled up with a chemical electrolyte between them, letting it hold roughly 100,000 times more charge than the kit's 22pF ceramic capacitor in a similar-sized package. That chemical construction is also why it only works with current flowing one direction; it is polarized.

hazards: installing it backwards (reverse polarity) or exceeding its 50V rating can cause it to heat up, bulge, vent, or in rare cases pop
do not touch a hot or visibly bulging capacitor
handling_notes: always check the negative stripe before powering the circuit
bend leads gently, not sharply right at the body, to avoid cracking the internal seal
common_mistakes: reversing polarity

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: capacitor feels warm, the top bulges, or there is a small pop or hiss
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: installed backwards or exposed to more than 50V
symptoms_and_causes.check: power off immediately, verify orientation against the negative stripe, and replace the part if the top is domed or leaking

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: circuit does not get the expected power smoothing
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: capacitor installed backwards, a bad solder or breadboard connection, or the wrong part substituted
symptoms_and_causes.check: use a multimeter's capacitance mode; expect a reading close to 10uF, and check continuity of both leads

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Discharge the capacitor first by briefly connecting a resistor across its leads, then set the multimeter to capacitance mode; expect a reading close to 10uF. Do not test an electrolytic on a diode or continuity setting expecting a simple short or open reading, since it will show a brief charging blip instead.
